The WHO guidelines for the screening, care, and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis C infection were updated in April 2016. These guidelines complement earlier WHO guidance on the prevention, care, and treatment of chronic hepatitis B and C infections. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections are significant global health concerns, with an estimated 240 million people living with chronic HBV and 110 million individuals testing positive for HCV antibodies, of whom 80 million have viremic infections. These infections disproportionately affect lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly in Asia and Africa. Even in low-prevalence areas, certain populations, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), individuals with HIV, and some indigenous communities, exhibit high levels of HBV and HCV infections. The advent of highly effective, well-tolerated oral treatment regimens with high cure rates after 12 weeks of therapy has revolutionized the management of chronic HCV infection. However, the high cost of these medications remains a significant barrier to access in many countries. Despite the global burden of HBV and HCV infections and the availability of effective treatments, most infected individuals remain unaware of their condition and often present with advanced disease. This low rate of hepatitis testing is attributed to limited testing facilities, lack of national policies or guidelines, expensive and complex diagnostic assays, and inadequate laboratory capacity and quality assurance systems. Testing and diagnosis of chronic HBV and HCV infections are critical for accessing prevention, care, and treatment services. Early identification of infected individuals allows for timely care and treatment to prevent or delay liver disease progression. Testing also provides an opportunity to link individuals to interventions that reduce transmission, such as counseling on risk behaviors, provision of prevention tools (e.g., sterile needles and syringes), and hepatitis B vaccination. These are the first WHO guidelines specifically addressing testing for chronic HBV and HCV infections. They aim to strengthen and expand current testing practices across all age groups and populations. The guidelines are organized into three sections: an introduction covering epidemiology and diagnostic assays, a summary of recommendations with evidence and rationale, and guidance for implementation at the country level. The recommendations include strategies for identifying individuals to test, testing approaches, and interventions to promote testing uptake and linkage to care. General population testing may be considered in areas with higher prevalence, and birth cohort testing can be applied to specific age groups with higher anti-HCV seroprevalence. Testing approaches should leverage existing facility-based (e.g., antenatal clinics, HIV or TB services) or community-based opportunities. For HBV, serological assays to detect hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) are recommended for diagnosing chronic infection. In settings with limited laboratory access, rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are recommended to improve access. Following a positive HBsAg test, nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HBV DNA is recommended to guide treatment decisions and monitor treatment response. Similarly, for HCV, serological testing for HCV antibodies is recommended, followed by NAT for HCV RNA to confirm viremic infection. Detection of HCV core antigen may be considered as an alternative to NAT in certain settings. The use of dried blood spot (DBS) specimens for serological and NAT technologies may facilitate access to testing in settings with limited facilities or expertise. Other interventions to promote testing uptake include peer and lay health worker support in community settings, clinician reminders in facilities, and integration of testing within drug treatment and harm reduction services. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of monitoring treatment response and disease progression in individuals with chronic HBV or HCV infections. For HBV, annual monitoring of ALT levels, HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels is recommended, along with non-invasive tests to assess for cirrhosis. For HCV, sustained virological response (SVR) after antiviral treatment completion is the primary indicator of treatment success. Implementation of these recommendations poses challenges, particularly in LMICs with limited access to diagnostic assays, antiviral therapies, and laboratory infrastructure. The guidelines provide a framework for country-level decision-making and planning to improve diagnosis and treatment rates, with the goal of identifying 30% of individuals with HBV and HCV infections by 2020 and 90% by 2030. Achieving these targets will improve clinical outcomes, save lives, reduce transmission, and prevent new infections.
